title: A request's time limit never takes effect in the real runtime
description:
Found by the scoped re-review of the fixes before the pin (2026-11-13). Not from that round: the line is unchanged since Task 4 (fortweb `0f93178`).

`app/runtime/roling.py` hands a Python function to the browser's `setTimeout` (`_fetch_or_none`, `timer = js.setTimeout(_abort, ...)`). Pyodide destroys such a function's proxy when the call returns, so when the timer fires the page logs "This borrowed proxy was automatically destroyed at the end of a function call. Try using create_proxy or create_once_callable." and nothing is aborted. The Python tests cannot see it (their stand-in keeps the callback and calls it), and no browser test waits for a request's time to run out.

Shown in the real page against the fixed build (session scratchpad `review-final-fix/evidence.md`, N1): a `source.json` held 15 s is still "Reading..." at 15 s; a server that answers after 25 s is read after 26 s; a server that does not answer for 100 s ends in the bridge's 75 s TIMEOUT, the worker discarded, and the unlock screen 75 s after pressing Open. So one unanswered request closes the vault, which is the harm the whole-feature review showed for a heavy source, reached another way.

The same round takes in three small things the reviewer noted: a role whose name is only a joiner is accepted; `cashier` plus a joiner is offered as an identifier name unnumbered beside an existing `cashier`; two behaviours of the bounded read have no test of their own.

## Acceptance Criteria

- In the real runtime a request that is not answered within its 10 s is aborted then and the read answers "Could not reach <host>."; the vault stays open and the wallet stays usable. Shown by browser tests that wait for it, for the source document and for a definition.
- The function handed to the timer lives until the timer fires or is cleared and is released afterwards; unit tests pin it, and their stand-in refuses a bare Python function.
- A role needs a name with a character that is neither white space nor a joiner; the numbering of an offered identifier name sees through joiners.
- Tests pin one derivation per target and that a derivation stops once it is over its budget.
- Python tests, type check, runtime build, the whole browser suite with pristine output and no file over 210 s, and the publication-workflow test pass; FortWeb CI on `dev` is green for the final commit; a scoped re-review passes.
notes:
Severity: high for availability (a host that does not answer closes the vault after 75 s; no data is lost and nothing is sent elsewhere). Confidence: high (reproduced by the reviewer in the real page, four probes). Evidence: review-final-fix/evidence.md section N1 and out/rr-hang*.out.
Fix round returned (2026-11-13): fortweb dev 53bff84..1555227, 7 commits, implementer status DONE. N1: the timer is handed create_proxy(_abort) and released exactly once after it was cleared or had fired (ed4232c); the unit tests' stand-in refuses a bare function; two browser tests in a new fortweb-roles-time.spec.ts wait for the real 10 s limit (the source document and one definition) and failed against 53bff84. N2: a role's name needs a character that is neither white space nor a joiner (a08fe3b). N3: the numbering of an offered identifier name leaves the joiners out on both sides (6a446db, 1555227). N4: tests for one derivation per target and for stopping over the budget, each failing under its mutant (5d99625). N5: the dialog's nine keyboard tests moved to fortweb-roles-dialog-keys.spec.ts (bf38113). Its own checks on 1555227: Python 220 OK, typecheck, build, browser suite 137 passed in 8.7 min (largest file 178.9 s), publication-workflow 14/14. Its one note: a body that stalls midway is covered by the Python tests only, because the routed fixture cannot send part of a body and then stall. Report: final-fix-2-report.md. Controller suite and scoped re-review are next.
Controller check on fortweb 1555227 (2026-11-13): Python 220 OK, typecheck clean, runtime built, browser suite 137 passed in 8.6 min (2 workers, 20 spec files, nothing failed, flaky or skipped, no slow-file notice, slowest file 182 s; the two time-limit tests take 39 s together), publication-workflow 14/14. FortWeb CI green for 1555227 (run 43363564393: 137 passed on one worker in 10.5 min, no slow-test annotation, no retry). The first scoped re-review, dispatched at the most capable tier, was cut off by the account's limit for that model before it reported; the session itself was held by the same limit until the owner said to continue on 2026-11-14. The re-review was dispatched again at the standard tier, so that it cannot stall on that limit again, and told to settle the security item by re-running the time-limit probes in the real page, not by reading. This departs from the skill's default tier for reviews; the reason is availability, and the evidence asked for is objective.
close_reason: Fixed in fortweb 53bff84..1555227: the browser's timer is handed a proxy that lives until the timer fires or is cleared and is released exactly once (ed4232c), so a request that is not answered is aborted at its 10 s and answers 'Could not reach <host>.'; a role's name needs a character that is neither white space nor a joiner (a08fe3b); the numbering of an offered identifier name leaves the joiners out on both sides (6a446db, 1555227); tests for one derivation per target and for stopping over the budget (5d99625); the dialog's keyboard tests in a spec of their own (bf38113). Scoped re-review PASS, with the security item shown in the real page over a real HTTPS server: a source document never answered ends at about 11 s with the sentence, a definition never answered ends at 10.9 s with its publication 'could not be read', the vault stays open in both, no proxy error is logged, and nothing is left behind per request (27 timers of a whole read each cleared and released once; cancellation paths probed). Controller suite green on 1555227 (Python 220, typecheck, build, browser 137 passed with no slow-file notice, publication-workflow 14/14); FortWeb CI green for 1555227 (run 43363564393). The re-review ran at the standard tier because the account's limit for the most capable model had been exhausted; its evidence is session scratchpad review-final-fix2/evidence.md.

title: Fixes before the pin: findings of the whole-feature review
description:
The whole-feature review of 2026-11-13 (fortweb `38d50ea..ca8b869`, most capable tier, with a real local HTTPS server) answered "not ready to merge". This bead is the one fix round for its findings, before Task 7 pins a wallet commit. The decisions are in the plan ("Fixes before the pin") and the design; the detailed list is `final-fix-1.md` in the plan's workspace. The held-Enter bug fortoid-7ji.3 is fixed in the same round.

Findings: C1 the no-cors probe follows redirects, so a source can send the wallet's requests to hosts never typed (26 requests reached another host in one read); C2 nothing bounds what an in-limit source costs: a 1 MB source froze the engine for 65 s and closed the vault, and after 13 take-ons of a heavy role (3 to 4 estimated on a phone) `roles.list` passed the bridge's 30 s and every unlock returned to the unlock screen; I1 "does not allow wallets to read it yet" cannot appear under the shell's COEP header; I2 an address or oobi the URL parser rejects ends in "Runtime request failed."; I3 text from a source can hide the host under My roles (a right-to-left override), look-alike identifier names, an empty role name; I4 every failure to get a definition is reported as an identifier mismatch; I5 the content-type rule is not mad-discovery's; M2-M5 smaller error-handling gaps.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every request a read makes is a cors request that refuses redirects, to the typed source's own files; no second request is made when one fails. A rejected read of the source document says "Could not read <host>: it cannot be reached, or it does not allow wallets to read it yet."; one not answered in time says "Could not reach <host>."
- The reviewer's heavy sources (400 publications; one responsibility relying 15,000 times on one definition) are read within the limits: at most 50 publications, each definition parsed once, at most 5,000 items in the answer, the clock checked for every publication.
- `roles.list` reads no stored definition; a role over 200 items or 200,000 bytes is refused with "<host> publishes more than the wallet keeps for one role." and nothing is written.
- `[example.org` and a malformed oobi no longer give "Runtime request failed.".
- No format character (Unicode Cf) in any string shown; a role needs a name that shows; under My roles the host has a line of its own before the publication's name.
- A definition that cannot be read gives `problem: "unreadable"` and "A definition from <host> could not be read."; a mismatch is only a failed SAID check.
- Content type: `application/json` or ending `+json`, parameters ignored.
- Only a fresh press of Enter takes on a role (fortoid-7ji.3).
- Python tests, type check, runtime build, the whole browser suite with pristine output and no file over 210 s, and the publication-workflow test pass; FortWeb CI on `dev` is green for the final commit; a scoped re-review passes.
notes:
Reviewer's full report and probes: session scratchpad final-review/review.md (and pw/, py/, srv/ beside it).

Controller's decisions are in the plan (Fixes before the pin) and the design (commit 73bed05). Fix list: final-fix-1.md (H1 = fortoid-7ji.3, K1-K11). One fix implementer dispatched on fortweb dev at ca8b869 (standard tier); a scoped re-review at the most capable tier follows. Not fixed here, by decision: a browser test against a real local HTTPS server (fortoid-7ji.5); M7 one guarded fixed wait in the last-read spec; M8 unit tests run on CPython 3.12 while the engine is Pyodide 3.14; M9 no confirmation before Remove (the design says one tap removes); isolating each source string inside a responsibility's line. M1 and M6 are answered in the design (differences from mad-discovery written down; what a read's request carries). The review's notes for mad-discovery are issues 2, 3 and 4 on its repository (beads fortoid-ksz, fortoid-016, fortoid-b3u).
Fix round returned (2026-11-13): fortweb dev ca8b869..53bff84, 17 commits, implementer status DONE_WITH_CONCERNS; every item H1 and K1-K11 addressed. Its own checks on 53bff84: Python 209 OK, typecheck, runtime built, browser suite 134 passed in 7.7 min (longest spec file 188.9 s, no split needed), publication-workflow 14/14. K5 was switched mid-round to mad-discovery Ruling 13 (a commit of its own, bf06c1c). Its concerns: (1) once, running the accessibility spec alone, the Foundation's test 'Create Identifier preserves validation, Cancel and safe fixture submission' failed; it passed in four later runs and both full suites and touches nothing of this round; (2) one assertion in fortweb-accessibility.spec.ts had to follow the new My roles line; (3) app/fixtures/data.ts has no unread member (the page treats a missing one as 0); (4) the pause between publications is tested in Python only; (5) the singular '1 more publication is not shown' has no test. Report: final-fix-report.md in the plan's workspace. Controller suite and scoped re-review are next.
Scoped re-review (2026-11-13, most capable tier, read-only, re-running the whole-feature review's reproductions against the fixed build over a real local HTTPS server): PASS. All twelve items resolved; K1, K2, K3 stated closed: a redirecting source got 27 requests, each address once, none reached the other host (was 53 and 26); 60 publications read in 158 ms and 5 MB (was 13.5 s and 926 MB), 400 in 147 ms (was 65 s and the unlock screen), another request answered in about 70 ms while a read derived; the heavy role is refused in the dialog and a role at the limits taken on eight times lists in 7 to 40 ms and survives lock, reload and unlock. Mutants for K6, K8, K10, K11 fail their tests. The refused character set equals mad-discovery's FORBIDDEN (214 code points, swept). The reviewer found one more defect, not on the list and older than the round (since Task 4): a request's 10 s limit never takes effect in the real runtime; filed as fortoid-7ji.9 and fixed before the pin. Smaller things the reviewer noted: Ruling 13 allows the joiners, so a role named with only a joiner is accepted and cashier plus a joiner is offered unnumbered (both taken into fortoid-7ji.9); two K2 behaviours have no test of their own (also taken in). The intermittent Foundation test 'Create Identifier preserves validation...' failed once for the reviewer too (then 10 of 10); its code path is not one this work changed. Correction: the request time-limit bug named above as fortoid-7ji.9 is bead fortoid-7ji.6.

title: Task 4: Reading a source over the network: `sources.read`
description:
Plan task 4 of .internal/plans/2026-11-12-first-browser-demonstration.md.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With the fixture source, `sources.read {address: "mad.example.test"}` returns host `mad.example.test`, 3 publications, `checked` 26, and the `dropin-class` publication's roles as in Task 3.
- `cors: false` gives the `UPSTREAM` error "mad.example.test does not allow wallets to read it yet."
- `tamper` on an rr of `class-brick` gives that publication `problem: "mismatch"` and no roles; the other publications that do not use it keep their roles.
- `oversize` gives "mad.example.test publishes more than the wallet reads in one go."
- An unroutable host gives "Could not reach <host>."
- `sources.read {address: "http://x"}` gives the `VALIDATION` error "That is not an address the wallet can open."
- Python unit tests cover the orchestration with a fake `fetch_bytes`: the 50-definition limit sets `problem: "limit"`, and the 60 s clock stops the read.
- `npm run typecheck` passes; the existing 60 browser tests still pass.

title: Startup Proof fails on main since wallet pin a083cea (runtime boot exceeds 30 s on the CI emulator)
description: Android API 36 Startup Proof has failed on every main run since the pin to seriouscoderone/fortweb a083cea (runs 53-60). Failure: 'FortWeb reported a fatal startup condition ... request_timeout method=vaults.list timeout_ms=30000', preceded by worker_invalidation reason='worker boot failed' (Runtime request timed out for worker boot). Passing run 51 (pin 4d40134): whole test took 26 s, so the emulator boots the runtime in about 20 s of a 30 s budget. Only startup difference on a fresh install in a083cea: the home route now renders the 'Starting your wallet...' page with an infinitely animated loading bar instead of the static splash. Emulator runs with -gpu swiftshader_indirect (software rendering). Hypothesis: the continuous 60 fps animation competes for CPU with the runtime boot and pushes it past 30 s.
acceptance_criteria: Root cause confirmed by experiment; fix has a regression test; Startup Proof green on main in CI.
notes:
2026-11-12 investigation. Evidence: run 60 logcat shows request_start vaults.list at 01:14:31.0, runtime_origin_contract_forwarded (worker alive) at 31.9, then nothing until worker_invalidation 'worker boot failed' at 01:15:01.1. Passing run 51 (pin 4d40134): 'Starting 1 tests' 19:39:50 -> 'Finished' 19:40:16, so boot took about 20 s. Emulator: 2 virtual cores (cpuinfo), -gpu swiftshader_indirect, and busy with first-boot system work during the window. a083cea did not touch runtime/bridge.ts; on a fresh install its only start-up change is the starting page with an infinite CSS animation (document.getAnimations() shows loading-bar-slide running, iterations infinite; the pre-existing page-fadein runs once). Not reproducible in headless desktop Chromium (5.48 s vs 5.50 s on 4 cores, 8.2 s vs 7.7 s on 1 core, within noise), so the emulator run is the test of the hypothesis. Fix: FortWeb 354f8f9 moves the bar on a 300 ms timer (4 positions, no animation or transition, timer stops when no bar shows, none under reduced motion); regression test in playwright/fortweb-fast-launch.spec.ts. Pinned in 704679d.
CI result for the 300 ms bar (pin 354f8f9, commit 704679d): Startup Proof run 61 PASSED, so removing the continuous animation fixes the timeout. But the test took 43.1 s; passing runs before the regression took 25.6-37.4 s (runs 38, 45, 46, 50, 51) and the failing runs 42.9-44.6 s, of which 30 s is the boot timeout. That puts the boot in run 61 at about 29 s of its 30 s budget on a slow runner (emulator boot 71 s). Each bar step is one drawn frame, so the bar was slowed to one step a second: FortWeb 47b10f4, pinned in 9a1be48.
Second sample of the 300 ms bar (dispatch run 62, fast runner): pass, test 32.1 s. One-step-a-second bar (pin 47b10f4, main 542d49d): Startup Proof run 63 PASSED with the test at 21.2 s, the fastest of all sampled runs (pre-regression passes: 25.6-37.4 s). All 10 workflows on 542d49d are green.
Correction: seven failed runs (53, 54, 56-60), not eight; runs 52 and 55 were cancelled by later pushes.
close_reason: Root cause confirmed on the CI emulator: the start page's infinite CSS animation drew a frame per refresh and starved the runtime boot (8 failing runs). Fix: the loading bar moves once a second on a timer, no animation (FortWeb 354f8f9 + 47b10f4, regression test in fortweb-fast-launch.spec.ts). Verified: Startup Proof run 63 green at 21.2 s; all 10 workflows green on main 542d49d.

title: Converge the SAID/KERI P2P requirements (v2) with the browser vision
description:
Owner's other thread: Claude doc 'SAID / KERI P2P Architecture: Updated Requirements (v2)'. Analysis 2026-11-11: it is the data layer (schemas by SAID, ACDC write grants, encrypted records, mailbox sync, adoption manifests, percolated OOBI discovery); docs/vision/authentic-web-browser.md is the host layer (where apps run, consent, per-app AIDs, hardware unlock). Its 'request interface (sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt)' == the vision's KERI API.

Decisions the owner needs to make before a merged spec:
1. Domains: required of every adopter (P2P) vs people without domains (browser). Proposal: only organizations publish from domains; people signal adoption to peers they exchange with.
2. One identity per person on a multi-device multi-sig group (P2P) vs one AID per app/relationship (vision); KERI delegation would link them publicly.
3. Put the app's code bundle SAID in the adoption manifest so it doubles as the app manifest.
4. Bridge parity: 11 Android-only bridge calls exist (device, biometric, keystore x4, secret x4, qr); FortWeb's native client has no iOS transport; P2P requires iOS and Android together.
5. Phone limits: the Python engine only runs in the foreground with the vault unlocked, so scheduled re-signing/background refresh happen at next unlock.
Also open in that doc: should only signed manifests count as adoption (its comment thread).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Owner decides 1-5
- One merged spec (vision + P2P) in docs/, with a first build slice chosen
notes:
OWNER DECISIONS 2026-11-11 (voice, restated):
1. Domains: like the WWW, people need no domain. Organizations publish schemas at their domains (OOBIs). A person types a web address into the KERI browser; it reads the OOBIs there, loads/understands the schemas, and percolates outward (other referenced domains), possibly in the background, depth maybe a setting. Wallets are nodes.
2. Identity: multi-sig is NOT planned (advanced feature; Sam Smith: pre-rotation + signing keys are enough for normal people). The P2P doc oversold it. Multi-device identity therefore has no mechanism yet (open, not blocking).
3. Model: published schemas = a TYPE (an application's interface, 'what it means to be a candlestick maker'), not tied to an AID. A wallet INSTANTIATES a type as its own AID (e.g. my candlestick-maker AID for the wax company). Deployed SERVICES have service AIDs; an org may publish hundreds of types and run services for only some. 'Interoperability by default' = open invitation to instantiate roles. Apps brought into the browser + where app code comes from: owner will supply a separate application document; do not design it yet.
4. iOS: in scope, make iOS ready too. Owner has a Mac and iOS simulators. Fork exists: seriouscoderone/fortios (last pushed 2026-07-21, needs syncing with upstream).
5. Phone limits: must be overcome; KERI mailbox expected to let the wallet go online/offline.
STILL OPEN on domains (asked owner): (a) is a person's instantiation visible/counted by anyone (the org, the public, nobody)? (b) does an unsigned schema file count as adoption or only a manifest signed by the org's AID?
HOLD: do not merge the specs until the owner's application document arrives.
OWNER DECISIONS 2026-11-11 (second round, voice, restated):
6. Devices: NO shared identity across devices. Each wallet instance (desktop, phone, web) is separate with its own AIDs. Multi-sig stays an advanced feature, not developed further now. This CLOSES the 'one identity on desktop and phone' open item (P2P requirement 9 is dropped).
7. Device fit may belong in type definitions: e.g. an accounting role suits desktop (spreadsheet integration); field roles suit a phone (photos, barcode scanning). Idea to carry into the application spec: a type can state which wallet/capabilities it needs; Fortoid's capability bridge is the natural check.
8. A person's instantiation is PRIVATE: nobody is told or counts it. Others learn the role only when the person acts in it. Credentials/licences for a role are separate applications run by other independent actors (ACDCs), not part of instantiation.
9. Publishing a schema on a domain IS the organization's authorization (presence is the vote). No signing of schemas; no requirement for a signed manifest for it to count. My suggestion to count only signed manifests is withdrawn; this answers the open comment in the P2P doc (bare file counts).
10. Versioning: a changed type is a new schema that links back to the schema it supersedes (owner's application document will define this). Note: with SAIDs the link must live in the NEW schema pointing back; the old schema cannot be edited to point forward.
Domains questions are now fully answered. Still waiting for the owner's application document before merging specs.
2026-11-12: Owner supplied the application-language documents (from a private repository): definitions are models, authorizations and responsibilities; a runtime instantiates responsibilities; the workbench is where the work happens. Merged vision drafted as a PRIVATE document for the owner's review; nothing from those documents is committed to this public fork until the owner says it may be. Open rulings for the owner: (1) shared-data semantics: actor model vs shared workspace; (2) the published form of definitions (the bundled KERI library only checks that a document's $id is its own SAID at an OOBI address, so all definition kinds could be served that way; FortWeb's entry point still rejects such addresses); (3) one AID per role taken on; (4) what a person sees after taking on a role; (5) whether the merged vision may be public; (6) catching up from the mailbox on next open. The public docs/vision/authentic-web-browser.md is stale in two places (apps as signed code bundles; multi-sig research) and will be rewritten once (5) is answered.
OWNER RULINGS 2026-11-12 (voice, restated):
11. Shared data: each node (wallet, browser, service) keeps its own data in its own local database next to its KELs and TELs; KERI's own database is the standard choice, any other local store is allowed. So there is no shared workspace; the actor model governs and the P2P design is plumbing. Checked in code: the wallet's KERI store is the browser-safe interface over IndexedDB (keri.db.webdbing/webbasing, keri.app.webkeeping); native KERIpy uses LMDB (keri.db.dbing).
12. Published form: all kinds of definition are published the same way, in whatever file format the designer project settles on.
13. Roles: a role is a collection of ACDC credentials; the AID that holds them can perform it. (Corrects my earlier 'one AID per role' reading; one AID can hold several roles, and all credentials a role needs must be issued to the same AID.)
Also: the owner's public repository mad-discovery is the publication and discovery work; not read yet, not attached to this session.
Still open: default AID when taking on a role (new vs reuse); what a person sees after taking on a role; whether the merged vision may be public; mailbox catch-up on next open.
OWNER RULINGS 2026-11-12 (second round, restated):
14. Missing credentials do not block taking on a role: the wallet shows a warning. An AID acquires the credentials over time, like earning certifications; the processes and schemas for acquiring them are expected to be published in the application language too.
15. Publication and discovery: use the owner's public mad-discovery project where it is compatible; where it is not OOBI compatible, update it.
16. The owner asked to make the KERI forks private for now. This replaces the 'may the merged vision be public' question.
MAD-DISCOVERY ASSESSMENT (public repo, README and docs/design.md read in full at 359a13a):
- A source is a plain static folder: source.json + definitions/<SAID>.json + pages/. Its address is an https URL ending /source.json. Every definition is checked byte for byte against its SAID (Blake3-256). Publications are unsigned offerings; a reader walks introductions from source to source. This supersedes the P2P design's /oobi/<SAID> publication paths and signed manifest, and matches rulings 9 and 12.
- Identity side is OOBI compatible: source.json may state 'by' (an AID) and 'oobi', which the wallet's existing OOBI resolver can resolve. The live test source (mad.seriouscoder.one: 3 publications, 26 served definitions) states neither yet.
- Definitions are NOT resolvable by the bundled KERI library as data OOBIs: it only fetches /oobi/<SAID> at the host root and checks a schema by $id, while a source serves definitions/<SAID>.json and the test definitions carry the SAID in 'd'. This matters only where a definition is used as an ACDC schema; mad-discovery's design already lists a keripy-shaped /oobi/<SAID> as a possible later extra.
- Two gaps for a wallet in a browser/WebView: the live source sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (checked with an Origin header), so a page cannot fetch it; and the reader's fetch routine is Node-only (session.ts imports fetchJson from fetch.ts).
- Proposed updates, awaiting the owner: (a) sources send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (alternative: the wallet fetches through a native bridge capability); (b) make the fetch routine injectable so the SAID check and the walk run in a browser; (c) optional /oobi/<SAID> copies, with the SAID in $id, for definitions used as ACDC schemas.
- First demonstration now targets the live test source: address box in the wallet -> read source.json -> list publications -> verify definitions -> take on a role, with a warning per missing credential.
PRIVACY FINDINGS (GitHub docs read 2026-11-12):
- A fork's visibility cannot be changed. Route: Settings > General > Danger Zone > Leave fork network (fork must be public, under 1 GB, no child forks; permanent), then change visibility to private. Git history is kept; the docs say issues, pull requests, stars, watchers and comments of the fork are not retained, and do not say what happens to a pull request the fork has open upstream (keri-foundation/fortweb#49). Alternative: bare clone, delete the fork, recreate it, mirror push; the docs warn that deleting a fork permanently deletes associated pull requests.
- Private repositories pay for Actions from the plan's included amount ($12 Free, $18 Pro; about 2,000 or 3,000 Linux minutes a month). One push to Fortoid main runs 10 workflows, about 43 billed minutes (measured on run 60), so roughly 46 pushes a month on Free. CI needs trimming before going private (emulator proofs manual or scheduled).
- If FortWeb goes private, Fortoid CI can no longer check it out (.github/actions/prepare-fortweb-runtime uses Fortoid's own token). The Demo APK step is continue-on-error, so the APK would ship WITHOUT the wallet and the proofs would fail. Needs a read-only deploy key or fine-grained token for FortWeb stored as a Fortoid Actions secret, and the checkout step wired to use it.
- The demo-latest APK on a private repository downloads only from a browser signed in to GitHub.
- This session cannot change repository settings; the owner does it.
17. 2026-11-12 (later): the owner dropped the privacy request after hearing what it takes ('Don't worry about making it private then'). The forks stay public. Consequence: material from the owner's private repositories stays out of these forks; the merged vision stays in the owner's private document until the owner says it may be published. The privacy findings above are kept for reference.
OWNER RULINGS 2026-11-12 (third round, voice, restated):
18. The wallet is a node; that node takes on responsibilities as an identity. The Roles page starts empty: no roles exist in a wallet until it has opened an address and read what an organization publishes.
19. Open protocol, in the spirit of Bitcoin's. Anyone may appoint themselves to any role (a gym owner included) and issue grants to others; a grant matters only to those who accept its issuer as an authority. Trust roots are the people one already knows and accepts. To be a company's cashier, that company's owner has to issue the grant, so a company first bootstraps its own authority. Confirms the 'Not appointed yet' warning.
20. Choosing an identifier for a role: offer 'create new' and 'select from existing' side by side, like the AWS console wherever a role is needed. (Answers the open question 'new AID or reuse'.)
21. Examples to explain the idea, later, in rising richness: an online shop (a person is only a customer), a ride-hailing service (customer or provider), a network-marketing company (many kinds of actor). Stay with the gym test data for now. The owner expects people to find the whole concept hard to grasp, so plain examples matter.
CORRECTION to ruling 19 (owner, 2026-11-12): it is NOT that anyone can appoint themselves to a role. Issuance follows the published definitions: some credentials are self-issuing (the holder issues them to itself), others must be issued by someone else. Openness means anyone may take part and trust comes from whom people accept, not that every role can be self-granted. Checked in the published test definitions: an rr carries 'issue' (the authorizations that responsibility issues, e.g. front-desk enrollment issues the enrollment authorization; cashier paid-admission and membership issue admission), but nothing marks a credential as self-issuing yet.
22. Owner, 2026-11-12: yes to the header. A source that wants browser wallets to read it sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *; mad-discovery's design is updated accordingly and the owner adds the header in CloudFront for the two live sources.

title: For the mad-discovery agent: refuse text that is not well-formed Unicode in source rules and catalog rows
description:
Ticket for the mad-discovery agent (the owner asked on 2026-11-12 that further changes to `mad-discovery` be logged as tickets for that agent, not made from the Fortoid session). It waits for the owner's ruling in fortoid-5wa.

## What is asked

A string taken from a stranger's file that is not well-formed Unicode (it holds an unpaired surrogate, for example the escape `\ud83d` alone) fails its rule, so the entry that holds it is dropped and counted like any other bad entry:

- in the source rules (`src/source.ts`: publication `name`, `description`, `tags`, `collection`, and any other string the document rules accept), so `source build` does not publish it and `verify` reports it;
- in the catalog build (`docs/plans/catalog-build.md`, Task 5: rows, index, sources), so no such string enters `said/<SAID>.json`, `index.json` or `sources.json`.

`String.prototype.isWellFormed()` is in Node 20 and later.

## Why

The wallet (fortweb `app/runtime/sourcing.py`, `_parse_bounded` with `_well_formed`) refuses any JSON file in which a string, member name or value, holds an unpaired surrogate. Such text cannot be stored or sent as UTF-8: the vault's store raised on it. A source document with one is "not a valid source"; a definition with one is not accepted.

`mad-discovery` accepts such strings today: `src/source.ts` lines 21 to 53 at `2eff6af` check length and C0/C1 control characters only. So:

1. a publisher can build and publish a source with `mad-discovery` that the wallet refuses whole;
2. in a catalog, a publication name with a lone surrogate from one source would be copied into a row and the index as an escape (`asciiJson`), and a wallet reading that file later would refuse all of it, including what other sources contributed. One source could make a row unreadable for wallets.

## For reference

- The wallet's rule and its tests: fortweb `app/runtime/sourcing.py` (`_well_formed`, `_parse_bounded`), `python/test_sourcing.py` (a surrogate in a value, in a member name, nested; a proper pair still reads).
- Where the wallet is stricter than `mad-discovery` is listed in Fortoid `.internal/specs/2026-11-12-first-browser-demonstration-design.md` ("Text rules, for the wallet only"). If this ticket is done, that line goes away for the surrogate rule.
- One edge to decide on the mad-discovery side: the wallet checks member names as well as values.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The owner has ruled (fortoid-5wa). If the ruling is no, this ticket is closed as not planned.
- If yes: the rule is in `mad-discovery`'s design and README rulings, the source rules and the catalog's row rules apply it, with tests for a lone surrogate in a publication name (dropped and counted) and for a proper pair (kept).
- The Fortoid side is told the commit, so the wallet's design can drop the difference.
